newsitem.title: CHINA: HK Democrats move out, unelected deputies move in.
newsitem.headline: HK Democrats move out, unelected deputies move in.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy politicians, kicked out of the legislature when China took over on July 1, left their offices on Thursday to make way for members of an unelected, Beijing-appointed assembly.
The new Provisional Legislature, meanwhile, rubber-stamped a government bill allowing illegal child immigrants to be deported back to mainland China.

The bill could mean the repatriation of hundreds, possibly thousands, of children who were smuggled into Hong Kong to join parents already with residency rights in the former British colony, now a quasi-autonomous region of China.
The new law, passed on Wednesday night, had created a storm of controversy after post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa asked the assembly to ram it through in a single sitting.
Traditionally new bills have received three readings spread over several sessions.
Martin Lee, leader of the largest party in the dissolved colonial chamber, was on hand to see aides finish packing their belongings into cardboard boxes ahead of the deadline to quit.

"This is a sad occasion," said Martin Lee, as his Democratic Party staff bade farewell to the offices, standing among desks littered with waste paper and plastic coffee stirrers. One aide was still transferring computer files on to disks.
The offices in Hong Kong's Central district belong to the government, which provided the legislators with much of their equipment too.
"Everything's being moved out, but not because we've lost an election," said Lee. "On the contrary. We won the last election to the Legislative Council in September 1995 for a four-year term."

As soon as Beijing reasserted control over Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, putting an end to 156 years of British rule, it disbanded the elected assembly and replaced it with a chamber made up of its own appointees.
Western nations and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong condemned the move, but in vain.
Lee said it was a "joke" that the Democrats and their allies were not sitting in the new Provisional Legislature, while candidates they defeated in the 1995 polls sat in their place.
Pro-democracy figures denounced the haste with which the interim assembly had passed the immigration bill, saying that it was already acting as a China-style rubber-stamp parliament.

"We think it is clearly unfair," said Lee, arguing that the new law contravened the post-handover constitution. By backdating the law's application to July 1, the day the new constitution took effect, the government had diluted rights conferred at that time.
His deputy, Yeung Sum, said Hong Kong's new chief executive must be very happy to have a "rubber stamp" legislature.
"I think that will make Mr Tung a very happy man because he will be pretty sure that whatever he tables will be passed," he said.

Tung's government did, however, drop plans to ram through another law immediately in similar fashion, this time one aimed at suspending a string of labour rights bills passed in the dying days of colonial rule.
It suggested tackling the bill at next week's sitting instead.
